correctness.rationale: Subtracting two equal-frequency multinomial count triples for P^r gives primitive collision lattice multiples of (−(B−A),B,−A). A nonzero collision needs r>=B; at r=B precisely the pair (0,B,0), (B−A,0,A) contributes, so Parseval gives m_B=D+2 binom(B,A)Re(c1^B conjugate(c0)^(B−A)conjugate(c2)^A e^{iθ})/S^B. The phase sign yields D+R cos(θ−φ) exactly. Writing xj=|cj|²/S, maximize strictly concave log product with exponents (B−A,B,A)/2: unique x=((B−A)/(2B),1/2,A/(2B)), and positive boundary gives zero contrast. At controlled θ=0,π/2, centered measurements equal R(c)(cosφ,sinφ), derivative inverse norm 1/R and deterministic maximum angle arcsin(δ/R), geometrically attained at tangent. Binomial mass inequality gives R*<=2^{1−B/2}; Stirling with A=(B−1)/2 gives balanced asymptotic. Independently enumerated integer collision witnesses and compared optimal ratios for every primitive A<B<=11; finite search supports not substitutes for all B proof.

value.rationale: The known first-resonance existence result assumes unimodular coefficients. This exact amplitude-allocation theorem answers a naturally motivated measurement-design question: how to distribute fixed Fourier power to maximize the first available intrinsic phase contrast and minimize inverse conditioning when only two controlled probes and known magnitudes are allowed. The sharp optimal allocation is strictly nonuniform, and exponential loss quantifies an intrinsic sensitivity limitation. The Lagrange optimization is elementary but is applied to a nontrivial exact collision-derived observable rather than an arbitrary numerical slice.
